channel.title: Segno devlog
channel.description: Progress notes on Segno, an open-source live looping appliance: the console, the audio engine, the firmware and the Flutter interface.

item.title: A take from the pedal, opened in Ableton Live
item.description: Segno now writes every recorded performance as an Ableton Live set, with a stem for each loop and the console's effects as plugins, and a Mac app opens it in Live in one click.
item.content:encoded:
Segno can record a whole performance, a take, while you loop. Until this week the take came out as finished audio: what the speakers played, plus each track as it sounded. That's fine for listening back, but not for working on the take later. This week the take became an Ableton Live set you can keep editing, and a small Mac app opens it in one click. Segno is still in development, and all of this runs on the bench console.

What gets recorded

First the console had to record the clean signal. Before #1809, a take tapped each input after its monitor chain, so an input played with monitoring off came out silent. Now every input monitored at arm, and every instrument with a patch, is also written raw, before its effects.

At the end of a take, the console renders stems from that recording and its event log. Since #1826, every lane of every looper track gets two: a dry stem, the loop as it played with nothing after it, and a wet stem, the lane after its volume, effects and mute. The console writes the Live set right after that render, at the end of every take.

The Live set

Each looper track is a Group track in Live. Inside it, each lane has a track that plays its dry stem through that lane's effects, and an "(as heard)" track with the wet stem, switched off, kept as a reference.

The effects are Segno's own. The console's effects code also builds as VST3 plugins, and #1811 loads each lane's chain into Live as those plugins, with the settings it had at arm. To check them I rendered a set of 31 tracks, one plugin each, from Live 12.2.7 and compared it with the engine's own render. 19 plugins were bit-identical, 5 were below -120 dBFS, and the other 7 were between -101 and -116 dBFS at their peak. Those 7 are bit-identical in our own test host, so the difference comes from rounding in Live's host. For a real take of 150 seconds, Live's render of the track was -139.6 dBFS (peak) away from what the console played.

A loop doesn't stand still while you play it, so #1839 replays the take's changes as Live automation: every effect switched on or off, every knob moved and every effect swapped in a slot. Each change is a step at the frame it happened. The same PR stopped the plugins from reporting a latency, because the console doesn't compensate one. With nothing reported, Live plays every lane with the same timing the console did.

The plugins also have a face now. #1819 gives each one an editor that draws its pedal the way the console's Effects page does, with every value printed, and Live's parameter list reads values the way the console shows them ("348 ms", "1/8D").

Getting it onto the Mac

Segno Transfer is the Mac app that browses and downloads takes from the console. Segno Transfer 0.3.0, released this week, adds Open in Live (#1830). It downloads the set and only the files it references, checks each one's SHA-256 against the console's copy, and moves the folder into place only after every file passes. On the bench, a take of 547 MB (the set and 11 audio files) came over in 17.5 seconds. A second click reused the verified copy in 10 ms.

The app carries Segno.vst3 and offers to install it when the set needs it and it's missing or older (#1831). The set is written as a Live Project folder (#1838), so Cmd+S saves it in place, and Open in Live now reopens your edited copy instead of downloading a fresh one (#1841).

Still open

The app and the plugin are signed locally, not notarized by Apple, so macOS asks you to approve each once in Privacy & Security. Live's own save of the reference set with the new Group tracks is still owed (#1826 explains the check), and Cmd+S saving in place still needs a check in Live 12.

item.title: Two fixes for ivi-homescreen
item.description: Segno's two screens turned up two bugs in ivi-homescreen, the Flutter embedder Segno runs on. One ignored a screen's pixel ratio, the other crashed the app on most shutdowns. Both fixes are now merged upstream.
item.content:encoded:
Segno's interface runs on ivi-homescreen, the Flutter embedder that Toyota Connected maintains for embedded Linux. On the console it draws straight to DRM/KMS: no Wayland, no desktop. The console has two screens, a 15.6-inch main screen and a 7-inch readout, and each screen is its own [[view]] in the embedder's config with its own Flutter engine. Both engines live in one process and share one Dart VM.

That setup turned up two bugs. I've been carrying a patch for each in Segno's Yocto layer, and this week I sent both upstream:

  • #859: apply the configured pixel ratio to window metrics
  • #860: keep the AOT snapshot mapped after engine shutdown

Why two engines

Flutter can draw several views from one engine, and ivi-homescreen supports that mode. In ivi-homescreen v3.0, only the first view receives input. The readout is the console's only touchscreen, so as a second view of a shared engine it could never be touched. With one engine per view, each engine is bound to its own output by connector name (HDMI-A-1, HDMI-A-2), and touch reaches the right view by the input device's name.

The two engines talk through the Dart VM they share. Each one publishes a SendPort in the IsolateNameServer under a fixed name and looks up the other's, with no plugin involved. The main screen owns the audio engine and all the state. The readout draws what it is sent and reports touches back.

Fix 1: the readout ignored its pixel ratio

The readout is a 1024x600 panel, and its view is configured with pixel_ratio = 1.6, so it should lay out at 640x375 logical pixels. It laid out at 1024x600 instead, with devicePixelRatio at 1.0, and everything on it was drawn too small.

The configured ratio did reach the engine, but only as a display property (View.of(context).display.devicePixelRatio was 1.6). Flutter lays out with the view's ratio, which comes from the window metrics, and on the backends without a Wayland window (drm-kms-egl, drm-kms-vulkan, software) the first window metrics always carried 1.0. Only the Wayland window ever changed that value.

The fix stores the configured ratio before the first window metrics are sent. Later resizes and the views added for extra DRM outputs read the same value, so they get it too. Touch input needed no change, because it is already delivered in physical pixels.

Fix 2: a crash on most shutdowns

Restarting Segno's service crashed the app on the way out. 12 of 16 stops left a core dump, all with the same crashing thread:

#0 stub CallNativeThroughSafepoint+0x58
#2 _libcRead.#ffiClosure3+0x70
#3 _readerMain+0xb8
...
#16 stub InvokeDartCode+0xd8

_readerMain is the isolate that reads the console board's serial link. It spends most of its time blocked in an FFI read() with a 100 ms timeout.

When an engine shuts down, ivi-homescreen called FlutterEngineCollectAOTData right after FlutterEngineShutdown. That unmaps the compiled Dart code. But shutting down an engine stops only its root isolate. Isolates the app started with Isolate.spawn keep running, the Dart VM keeps running (the other screen's engine is still on it), and the serial reader is usually sitting inside read(). When that call returns, it returns through a stub that is no longer mapped, and the process dies with SIGSEGV.

The fix leaves the AOT data mapped and lets the process exit release it. After the change there were 0 core dumps in 226 stops, and a clean stop takes about 0.35 seconds. One stop on the first patched build hung until systemd killed it. It didn't happen again in the next 150, and I don't know yet whether it's related.

Testing

Both branches build at ivi-homescreen v3.0 with gcc 14 and clang 19 and pass the project's 44 unit tests, its format, spelling and config-reference checks, and clang-tidy on the changed files. The on-device results above come from Segno's console: a Raspberry Pi 5 running drm-kms-egl, with both screens connected.

When this entry was first published, both pull requests were waiting for review, and Segno applied the same two patches in its Yocto layer until they were merged.

Update, 17 November 2026

Both pull requests were merged upstream on 17 November 2026. Segno now builds ivi-homescreen from the upstream v3.0 branch with both fixes in it, and no longer carries either patch.
